title: Just sitting
hook: a cushion, a wall, and no technique at all: Zen's sitting practice

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the science block with the line solid and light: keep what's solid, hold the rest lightly. Now a new block opens, the world's schools of practice, starting with Zen.

A round cushion on the floor. A plain wall a few feet away. Someone sits down, crosses their legs, rests their hands in their lap, and then nothing else happens. No counting the breath. No phrase to repeat. No candle, no picture to hold in the mind. A person just sits there, awake. That can sound like waiting for the real thing to start. In one Zen school, this is the real thing, and the Japanese teacher Dogen gave it a name almost too plain to be a teaching: just sitting.
screen: `A CUSHION. A WALL.` → `NO TECHNIQUE AT ALL.` → `JUST SITTING.`

segments.voice: Back on day one hundred three, the word zen turned out to mean meditation. Zazen is Zen's word for seated meditation, and Dogen's name for the way he taught it was shikantaza, usually put into English as just sitting. First, it has no technique. The last block met practices with a job to do: count the breath, note the thought, scan the body. Just sitting sets the jobs down. Second, the body does the work. In his short guide to zazen, Dogen's instructions are physical and plain: sit on a cushion, cross the legs, fold the hands, keep the back upright, don't lean left or right, forward or back. Eyes stay open, resting gently. Breath goes quietly through the nose. Third, thoughts. They will come. Dogen doesn't say to fight them or to follow them. His advice, in paraphrase: when a thought arises, notice it, and in the noticing it goes. He passes on an old exchange, too: asked what you think about while sitting, a teacher answers, roughly, think of not-thinking. And how do you do that? Non-thinking. It's meant to puzzle a little. Fourth, the surprise: for Dogen, sitting isn't a tool for getting enlightenment later. He taught that practice and awakening aren't two separate things; the sitting is already what it's looking for. Hard to hold in your head, which may be why he kept handing people a cushion instead of an argument. The Soto school, which traces itself to Dogen, puts just sitting at its heart. Rinzai Zen also sits zazen, and often adds something else to the cushion. That's tomorrow.
screen: `A SITTING WITH NO TECHNIQUE.` · `BACK UPRIGHT, EYES OPEN, BREATH QUIET.` · `A THOUGHT COMES: NOTICE, AND IT GOES.` · `NOT A TOOL. THE SITTING ITSELF.`

segments.voice: On a chair is fine: feet on the floor, back upright but not stiff, hands in your lap, eyes open and resting softly on the floor a little ahead. Breathe through your nose and leave the breath alone; when a thought shows up, notice it, and come back to sitting. There's nothing to get right, and another day, ten minutes is a good next step.
Zazen. Seated meditation in Zen. In Dogen's way of teaching it, just sitting, with nothing added. Today's word.
Your line: just sitting. Nothing added to it, and nothing missing from it. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Soto Zen, practitioners sit zazen as shikantaza, upright with eyes open and no object of focus, often in a meditation hall together and at set times of day.

notes: Editor pass: varied the repeated 'turned four ways' teach frame; changed 'to a lot of us' to avoid speaking for the listener.

Posture instructions (cushion, crossed legs, folded hands, upright, not leaning, eyes open, quiet breath through the nose) are paraphrased from Fukanzazengi; confirm the details, especially 'through the nose'.

The thought advice ('when a thought arises, notice it; in the noticing it goes') and the 'think of not-thinking ... non-thinking' exchange (attributed to Yaoshan, passed on by Dogen) are paraphrased; confirm attribution and wording.
The oneness of practice and awakening (shusho itto) is drawn from Bendowa; confirm the plain-language summary.
Soto/Rinzai framing: Soto traces itself to Dogen and centers shikantaza; Rinzai also sits zazen and often adds koans. Confirm fairness.
The outline's '13th-century Japan' was left out under the claims rule. The outline practice is ten minutes; the app sit is two, so ten minutes is offered as an optional next step.
